source.title: Looped Transformers with Source-Centered State Evolution
source.authors: Bum Jun Kim; Kohei Hayashi; Shunsuke Kamiya; Masanori Koyama; Yusuke Iwasawa; Yutaka Matsuo

record.file_problem: No apparent file problem; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares language-model architectures at matched parameter scales and reports held-out perplexity, bearing on whether architecture choices change loss only slightly. It does not fit or test scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The study evaluates recurrent-depth architectures and reports many PPL results. Those results bear on V4's architecture-sensitivity claim, but not on power-law scaling in parameters, tokens, or compute, extrapolation from scaling fits, compute-optimal allocation, other modalities, downstream scaling predictability, or fit-dependent scaling exponents. Reported PPL values used to choose hyperparameters are not treated as separate outcomes.
record.test_reason: The study proposes a looped-Transformer recurrence (SCSE) and compares it with its own shared-block baselines on perplexity. It cites Kaplan et al. and Hoffmann et al. only in the introduction. It fits no scaling law and runs no depth/width shape sweep of standard Transformers at fixed parameters. Its architecture comparisons are method-versus-baseline results, the kind that should not be rows. They also concern recurrence parameterisation and evaluation at untrained loop depths, not the shape variation V4 names. No version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that source-centered recurrence (learned anchor plus deviation-coordinate recurrence) improves the controlled shared-block quality frontier, with the clearest gains at deep extra-loop depths. The gains are not uniform: the tuned adapter is slightly better at T=8 in 50k-step C4, and the step-conditioned adapter is better at T=8 on 50M held-out OpenWebText.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies a different question and method from scaling-law fitting: it compares recurrent-depth architecture variants and measures held-out perplexity, without fitting parameter/token/compute power laws.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported PPL depends on architecture choice, parameter scale, and evaluation loop depth; within a method, PPL can also change between the training loop-depth range and extra-loop evaluation.

fits_no_version.finding: In shared-block looped LMs at matched scale (22M-95.6M), recurrence parameterisation changes WikiText-103 PPL substantially. At 22M, T=8: looped baseline 179.8 vs adapters/SCSE about 155-158. Evaluating at loop depths beyond training raises PPL for all methods.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Recurrence parameterisation in weight-shared looped Transformers changes loss substantially at fixed parameter count, unlike shape changes in standard Transformers.

record.problems: The evidence is limited to controlled shared-block language-model settings and the tested scales; the authors state that frontier-scale and billion-parameter/billion-token behavior remains open. The results do not constitute a broad sweep of depth and width or a scaling-law analysis.
record.rows_left_out: Additional architecture comparisons and results across WikiText-2, web corpora, held-out transfer, LAMBADA, longer contexts, longer training, and C4 scales are omitted; the 22M/50M/95.6M WikiText-103 matched-scale comparisons in Appendix Table 5 and Table 1 provide the selected fixed-scale architecture evidence. Also omitted are mechanistic diagnostics that do not measure the architecture-sensitivity outcome named by V4.

untested.parts: No power-law fit of loss in parameters, tokens or compute.
No sweep of depth/width/shape for standard Transformers at fixed parameter count. Only comparisons of the authors' recurrence against shared-block controls.
No other modalities or regimes fitted with power laws.
No analysis of downstream predictability from scale or loss.
No fitted exponents compared across setups.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V4 'challenges' label is dropped. The rows are the authors' method and baselines compared with each other, not a shape sweep. The variants change recurrence structure and add modules, and many rows evaluate at untrained loop depths. Scaling-law papers appear only as introductory citations; the limitations section says billion-parameter scaling-law behavior remains open.

versions.untested_parts: Power-law loss scaling in parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of much larger runs from power-law fits on small runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and its trend with compute.
No broad sweep of depth, width, and architecture families; comparisons are mainly among selected shared-block designs and controls at the stated scales.
Other modalities and the listed nonstandard training regimes.
Predictability of downstream performance from scale or pretraining loss.
Sensitivity of fitted scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocations to setup and fitting choices.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Matched-scale WikiText-103 shared-block comparisons at 22M, 50M, and 95.6M, over the reported loop depths
reader_labels.reason: The paper reports substantial PPL differences among architecture variants, including substantially stronger capacity-matched/tuned or recurrent-step-conditioned designs than the looped baseline; see r02-r04, r06-r08, r10-r12, r14-r16, r18-r19, r21-r22, r24-r25, r27-r29, r31-r33, and r35-r37.
